clue.text: Opponent's for change, not against

indicators.note: the letters are offered up to be changed into something else

explanation.surface: Someone describes a rival who has come round to supporting reform.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that an antagonist is exactly the person who is against, so the fodder denies the answer it spells.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both name the person on the other side of a fight or argument.

clue.text: Rude, coarse artist becoming accepted by Society

indicators.note: becoming means one piece turns into another, the artist changing into the socially accepted mark

parts.note: something coarse is rough to the touch, abrasive
RA is a Royal Academician, a crossword staple for artist
U stands for upper-class, the socially acceptable usage in the old U and non-U labels

explanation.surface: A crude painter finally wins acceptance among the upper classes.
explanation.walkthrough: In ABRASIVE the artist RA is 'becoming' U. U versus non-U was a 1950s label for upper-class and not-upper-class speech, and crosswords still use U for socially acceptable.
explanation.definitionFit: Rude words hurled in anger are abusive ones, insulting and offensive.

clue.text: "Excite a little" — that encapsulates it

indicators.note: to excite is to agitate, and agitated letters will not stay in the order given
the anagram holds IT inside

explanation.surface: A dictionary-style gloss, with a remark that the phrase sums the word up.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: 'excite a little' really does sum up titillate, and the same words stirred round IT build it.
explanation.definitionFit: To titillate is to excite mildly, often in a teasing way.

clue.text: Spears raised regularly during spear song

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifted means read bottom to top
the letters come from inside the phrase that follows
at regular intervals, so the letters are taken at a steady every-other spacing

explanation.surface: Warriors lift their spears in time with a battle song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spears' is used twice with different jobs: the first is the definition, a verb; the second is raw letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: a bull's horns pierce the way a spear does.

clue.text: Note doughnut with new taste, possibly rhubarb

parts.note: taste is one of the senses

explanation.surface: A baker notes a doughnut with a new flavour, perhaps rhubarb.
explanation.walkthrough: Rhubarb is British slang for nonsense, as well as the fruit the surface wants for a doughnut filling.
explanation.definitionFit: Talking rhubarb means talking nonsense.

clue.text: Copper on radio for so long

indicators.note: heard, not seen: the letters are spoken

parts.note: Cu is copper's chemical symbol, spoken as two letters

explanation.surface: A police officer lingers on the airwaves for ages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' wants to be a policeman on the radio; it is the element Cu, said aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are casual goodbyes.

clue.text: Clobber game when it retreats

indicators.note: an army that retreats goes back the way it came, so the game is read backwards

parts.note: brag is a card game like poker

explanation.surface: Beat the opposition, then back off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clobber' looks like a verb, to hit; here it is the British noun for clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Clobber is British slang for clothing or gear, as is garb.

clue.text: Sailors having a party on top deck

indicators.note: in a down clue, the party sits above the sailors

explanation.surface: The crew throw a party up on the top deck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deck' is a verb here, to decorate, not part of a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Deck in its decorating sense, as in 'deck the halls', is a synonym.

clue.text: Pirate needing repair to globe

indicators.note: the letters are broken and must be put back together

explanation.surface: A buccaneer patches up a battered globe, or map of the world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pirate' is an adjective or verb: pirate copies are bootleg copies.
explanation.definitionFit: Pirate and bootleg both describe illegally copied goods.

clue.text: Dispenser of drams? One article which might replace glasses

definitions.note: a relative clause standing for 'one who might replace glasses'

parts.note: an optic is the upturned-bottle measure behind a bar

explanation.surface: A bar's spirit measure is so handy it might stand in for glasses.
explanation.walkthrough: British pubs pour spirits through an optic, a measure clipped to an upside-down bottle. The surface wants glasses for drinking; the definition means spectacles.
explanation.definitionFit: An optician fits and replaces spectacles.

clue.text: Remark companion's missed by complete accident

indicators.note: the companion is left out of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Someone notes that a friend's comment went unheard in a total mishap.
explanation.walkthrough: CH, Companion of Honour, is a British order; dropping it from CHANCE leaves ANCE.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: anything spoken aloud counts, a remark included.

clue.text: Still passionate in chamber?

indicators.note: one word goes inside the other

parts.note: a po is a chamber pot

explanation.surface: Is the ardour still there behind the bedroom door?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' wants to be an adverb; it is a noun, a still photograph. PO is British for a chamber pot.
explanation.definitionFit: A still is a single photograph, often from a film.

clue.text: Ticks over icons on mobile?

indicators.note: heard down a phone line, so spoken rather than written

parts.note: icons = idols, said the same way

explanation.surface: A phone user taps checkmarks over the app icons on the screen.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'icons on mobile' about app symbols; the mobile is a phone you speak into, and the icons are idols.
explanation.definitionFit: Motoring idiom: an engine running slowly in neutral both ticks over and idles.

clue.text: Sensitive English poet originally appointed Laureate

indicators.note: take the first letter of each word that follows

explanation.surface: A thin-skinned English poet was first appointed Poet Laureate.
explanation.walkthrough: Andrew Motion was Britain's Poet Laureate, which the surface nods to.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe someone quickly moved by feelings.

clue.text: See about crossing Alps getting fresh passes

indicators.note: goes across the other word, holding it
as in 'about turn', the word faces the other way
something freshened is made anew, so the letters come out in a new order

explanation.surface: A traveller crossing the Alps finds fresh mountain passes to see.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passes' is a verb, as time passes, not mountain passes.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb synonym used of time: the weeks slip by, or go past.

clue.text: Clean egg is in return packaging

indicators.note: the egg and is go inside the packaging

parts.note: an SAE (stamped addressed envelope) is the packaging sent for a reply to come back in
a nit is the egg of a louse

explanation.surface: An egg is found sitting inside some returned packaging that needs cleaning.
explanation.walkthrough: SAE, the stamped addressed envelope enclosed for a reply, is a British convention; NIT and IS sit inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To sanitise something is to make it hygienic by disinfecting it, so the verb matches clean.

clue.text: Merciless leader restricts team socialising

indicators.note: to restrict is to confine, so the leader's name closes round the team

parts.note: Ming the Merciless, villain of Flash Gordon
eleven players, as in a cricket or football XI

explanation.surface: A harsh manager stops the players going out together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Merciless leader' looks like it wants M, the first letter; it is a whole character, Ming the Merciless.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a party host hopes guests will mingle and chat.

clue.text: Halal shin's prepared as God would have it

indicators.note: the letters are made up into something new

explanation.surface: A cut of halal meat is butchered as religious law requires.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface stays in Muslim practice, which is where the answer, Arabic for 'if God wills', comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: Inshallah means 'if God wills it'.

clue.text: Coinage of novel phrase about Northern Line

indicators.note: about means the rearranged phrase goes around the northern letter
novel means new, and a new version of the phrase has its letters reordered

explanation.surface: A new expression coined about London's Northern Line on the Tube.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coinage' suggests a newly invented word, which the surface backs up; here it means loose coins, which the British call shrapnel. The Northern Line is a London Underground route.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrapnel is British slang for small change, a pocketful of low-value coins.

clue.text: They might be Rick's family mugs

definitions.meaning: Rick Stein is a British TV chef; think of his surname in the plural

explanation.surface: A chef's relatives are gullible fools.
explanation.walkthrough: Rick Stein is a well-known British TV chef. 'Mugs' reads as fools after 'family', but means beer tankards.
explanation.definitionFit: A stein is a large beer mug, and the Steins would be Rick Stein's family.

clue.text: Salmon, company reared on island in case of shortage

indicators.note: in means the pieces sit inside the case letters
the case of a word is its outside, its first and last letters

parts.note: the word shortage, whose outer letters form the case

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means placed above the next piece
reared means raised up, so in a down entry the letters read upwards

parts.note: a key or cay is a low island

explanation.surface: A fishing company is set up on an island in case supplies run short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reared' turns the company abbreviation upward, and it sits 'on' (above) the island; all that goes 'in' the 'case of' shortage, its first and last letters. Key is also the word in Florida Keys.
explanation.definitionFit: The sockeye is a species of Pacific salmon prized for its deep red flesh.

clue.text: Cutter, when returned, secured by husband and wife

indicators.note: secured by means held fast between the husband-and-wife letters
returned means sent back, so the word reads backwards

parts.note: as can mean when, as in 'as I left'

explanation.surface: A married couple lock up a tool once it has been given back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Husband and wife' reads as a couple, but gives H, AND and W, with the 'returned' when slipped inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A handsaw is a saw worked with one hand, a kind of cutting tool.

clue.text: Eavesdrop on women fronting independent pop-up!

indicators.note: the women and independent go first
in a down clue, read upwards

explanation.surface: Snoop on women running an independent pop-up shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop-up' is split: pop is father, PATER, and up turns it round. Pater is an old British public-school word for father.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: tapping a phone line is electronic listening-in.

clue.text: One making predictions tipped paddleboat?

indicators.note: loses its tip, the first letter

parts.note: a small round boat paddled by one person; C removed

explanation.surface: A fortune-teller forecasts that a paddleboat will capsize.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tipped' suggests capsized, which fits a boat; it means the top letter is lopped off.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient Greece a prophet such as the one at Delphi foretold events, hence any predictor.

clue.text: It's relaxed, with 'ace' fare?

indicators.note: the letters are loosened and rearranged

explanation.surface: A laid-back eatery with excellent food.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: a casual place serving good food.
explanation.definitionFit: A cafeteria is an informal self-service eating place.

clue.text: Carry on investing roubles in flutter

indicators.note: to invest money is to put it into something

parts.note: R, the first letter of roubles, as on price tags

explanation.surface: Keep gambling roubles on a flutter, a small bet.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is finance: investing roubles, a flutter as a bet. 'Carry on' means to flirt, as in carrying on with someone.
explanation.definitionFit: British idiom: carrying on means dallying romantically with someone.

clue.text: Ex-PM in retreat following book

indicators.note: the retreat comes after the book

explanation.surface: A former prime minister goes into retirement after a memoir.
explanation.walkthrough: Tony Blair was UK Prime Minister 1997-2007. 'In retreat' reads as withdrawing, but 'in' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Tony Blair is a former British Prime Minister.

clue.text: Shout half-heartedly downstairs

indicators.note: half of the heart, the middle LL, goes

parts.note: one of the two middle Ls removed

explanation.surface: Someone calls down the stairs without much enthusiasm.
explanation.walkthrough: BELLOW's heart is LL; losing half of it leaves BELOW.
explanation.definitionFit: An adverb synonym: going downstairs takes you to the floor beneath.

clue.text: Multiple terms of reference rule out issues

indicators.note: something ruled out is excluded

parts.note: a remit is a body's terms of reference; plural
R, the abbreviation for rule, taken out

explanation.surface: Committees with several briefs dismiss certain topics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rule out' looks like a phrase meaning exclude; it splits into R and 'out'. 'Issues' is a verb, not topics.
explanation.definitionFit: To emit is to issue or send out.

clue.text: Walls of chapel best trimmed with romantic illumination

definitions.note: the clue's noun phrase stands for the adjective describing a room lit that way

indicators.note: walls stand around a building, so the chapel's walls go around the joining word
of here takes the outer letters, the walls, of the word chapel

parts.note: with means and, joining things together

indicators.note: trimmed cuts the last letter off the word for the best

explanation.surface: A chapel's finest walls are decorated with romantic lighting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Walls of' pictures the chapel's outside letters standing round the conjunction that 'with' supplies, as walls stand round a room.
explanation.definitionFit: Lighting by small flames from wax tapers is the classic romantic glow of a dinner for two.

clue.text: Swallows perhaps settle nose to tail

indicators.note: nose to tail means the front letter of the word moves round to the back

parts.note: a settle is a high-backed wooden bench, a seat

explanation.surface: Swallows, the birds, settle in a line one behind another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swallows' wants to be birds; it is a verb. 'Nose to tail' sends the first letter of SEAT to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To swallow food is to eat it, so swallows and eats are the same verb form.

clue.text: Moor vessel, checking bows essentially in order

parts.note: a fell is a hill or moor in northern England

indicators.note: the essence, the middle letters

explanation.surface: A ship is moored with her bows checked and everything shipshape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moor' wants to be the verb, to tie up a vessel; it is a noun, open upland. 'Order' means a society, not tidiness.
explanation.definitionFit: Both name a brotherhood of members bound by shared rules, as in a religious or chivalric order.
